messages.content: You are an expert space systems engineer providing detailed technical specifications.

You are synthesizing technical specifications from 3 AI models for "MW-class Cargo Tugs" in the context of Phase 0 - Space Resource Processing.

## Phase 0 after the 2026 re-assessment (binding context)

The original Phase 0 plan (a central 50 kt/yr processing station at Sun–Earth L4/L5, crew visits,
production LOX/LH₂, 100 kW-class freighters) was found not to close and is abandoned. Design for the
revised architecture below. Do not re-propose the abandoned design.

### Agreed by all three re-assessment models
- Split Phase 0 into 0A (research + pathfinders) and gated 0B (industrial): Structure agreed; budgets → §3 (All three)
- Abandon 50 kt/yr central SEL4/L5 ore processing: — (All three)
- Co-locate at least beneficiation and primary processing at the target NEA; ship product, not ore: Reference architecture (All three. GPT: "favoured but not universally optimal". Claude retains a central station fed with ≥20:1 concentrate as an alternative. Gemini's own weighted QOC scores SEL1 marginally higher (see §6).)
- Narrow product to native/reduced Fe-Ni; defer solar-grade Si and oxide-derived Al/Si: Fe-Ni baseline; Al/Si pilot or deferred (All three)
- Delivered product scale of order 1 kt/yr: 0.6–2.5 kt/yr (Claude 0.6–2.2 (central 1.3); Gemini 1.0–2.5 (1.5, of which 0.3 is water); GPT 0.6–1.0 contracted (0.67–1.33 capacity))
- MW-class cargo tugs: 1.0–2.5 MWe each; 10–18 tugs; 150–300 t payload (→ §3 for point values)
- Robots powered by HV tether from site power, with onboard battery for mobility and safe-mode: 1–3 kV; battery 10–50 kWh (Claude 2–3 kV, 10–30 kWh; Gemini 1–3 kV, 15–25 kWh; GPT 20–50 kWh, voltage unspecified)
- Delete the 200–500 MWh Li-ion line; size storage per site: 0.5–15 MWh total (Claude 0.5–3 MWh + thermal; GPT 1.3–3.3 MWh; Gemini <15 MWh (YAML 10 MWh))
- Reject $5/W array pricing: Hardware ~$30–150/W, launch separately accounted (Claude $30–150/W hardware ($50–230 installed incl. launch); Gemini $60–100/W (spec $75, range $50–110); GPT $30–100/W allowance ($45–220 with delivery))
- Replace 32–50 × 100 kg monoprop prospectors: Remote survey + 4–10 EP rendezvous scouts of 200–600 kg (All three agree a monoprop bus has ~0.5–0.8 km/s Δv. Remote-survey method differs (→ §3).)
- Add an Earth-to-space launch/delivery line: Line agreed; magnitude → §3 (All three)
- Add a comms, ground segment and mission-operations line; DSN not assumed free: Line agreed (All three. Claude and GPT reject the round-1 2.5 TB/day (~230 Mbps) figure.)
- Phase 0 uncrewed; remove habitat and quarterly visits: 0 crew visits (All three. Claude and GPT reject the "human-rating" label in favour of structural reserve plus docking/servicing interfaces. Gemini keeps docking ports and structural margins without commenting on the label.)
- Add an EP propellant supply line; xenon not baselined: Line agreed; demand → §3 (All three)
- No production LOX/LH₂ in Phase 0: — (All three. Claude and GPT remove the EML1 depot; Gemini "defers" cryo depots to 0B/Phase 1.)
- Add NRE, pathfinder, spares and contingency lines: Lines agreed; values → §3 (All three)
- Write a full organization (bom-0-7) specification: ~$100–350M (Claude $100–300M; Gemini $150–250M (text $200M); GPT $150–350M)
- Add a debris/contamination requirement and budget tighter than 99%: $50–300M (Threshold → §3)
- Freeze one configuration-controlled baseline; mark legacy documents superseded: — (All three)
- Earth-supplied material as a fallback if microgravity metallurgy fails: — (All three. Ranking relative to lunar → §3.)
- Tie Phase 0 output to Phase 1 demand with a material/purity/date specification: — (All three)
- Add waste-heat rejection (radiators) explicitly: Item agreed; sizing → §3 (All three)

### Owner decisions
- D-01 (accepted 2026-10-12): Fund 0A. Hold 0B as a gated real option, sized at the gate by signed Phase 1 demand. Call Phase 0 a capability programme, not a cost saving.
- D-02 (accepted 2026-10-12): Hybrid: NASA life-cycle gates with TRL/AD² for each critical technology, plus four discriminating gates (target, demand, economics, licence). Stringency follows reversibility.
- D-03 (proposed; treat as interim): Set an ALARP requirement with an interim design ceiling. The number itself goes to modelling, tests and the licensing state.
- D-04 (proposed; treat as interim): Use SEL1 as the reference case. Re-decide jointly with Phase 1 at the 0B gate.
- D-05 (proposed; treat as interim): Select no propellant yet. Cost iodine as the reference case and argon as the alternate, pending the supply audit and life tests. Water EP stays a desk study until a C-type target is confirmed.

Under D-02, KDP-0B (the one-way commitment to 0B production) needs every project-ending technology
at TRL 6 in a relevant environment with no waivers; internal 0A milestones need TRL 4–5.

### This item: bom-0-4 MW-class Cargo Tugs (0B)
Accepted scope: Electric-propulsion cargo tugs of 1–2.5 MWe with 150–300 t payloads, carrying product from the NEA to the delivery node.

Round-2 proposals for this item (per model; not approved as numbers):
- resize · bom-0-4 cargo tugs · supported by all · quantity: Claude 12 @ 1–1.5 MWe incl. arrays; Gemini 14 @ 2 MWe; GPT 10 @ 2 MW excl. arrays · cost: Claude $150–350M; Gemini $180–260M; GPT $150–350M · confidence: medium (Claude); high (Gemini, power); low (GPT)

- T02 MW-scale deployable solar arrays (tug; site per Gemini and GPT): TRL 2–4 now, target 6, AD² 5, project-ending
- T03 MW-class waste-heat rejection (plant and tug): TRL 2–5 now, target 6, AD² 5–6, project-ending
- T12 Autonomous handling, docking and transfer of 150-300 t payloads: TRL 2–4 now, target 6, AD² 5–6, architecture-change
- T14 Propellant storage and feed at hundreds of tonnes per tug: TRL 2–4 now, target 6, AD² 5–6, project-ending
- T25 Target-local and SEL1 cargo-node navigation and control: TRL 2–4 now, target 6, AD² 4–6, project-ending

Other Phase 0 items (do not duplicate their scope): bom-0-1 Prospecting Survey and Rendezvous Scouts; bom-0-2 Mining Robots; bom-0-3 Processing Plant at the Target NEA; bom-0-5 Site Power, Arrays and Storage; bom-0-6 Water Pilot (C-type target only); bom-0-7 Organizational Infrastructure; bom-0-8 Earth-to-Space Launch and Delivery; bom-0-9 Communications and Ground Segment; bom-0-10 Mission Operations; bom-0-11 NRE, Ground R&D and Qualification; bom-0-12 0A Pathfinder Demonstrator; bom-0-13 Phase 1 Receiving Node (SEL1); bom-0-14 Spares and Replacements; bom-0-15 Debris and Contamination Control; bom-0-16 Electric-Propulsion Propellant Supply; bom-0-17 Contingency and Reserve.

State quantities and costs as ranges with their basis, split 0A and 0B where the item spans both,
and say where you disagree with the round-2 figures and why.

## Model Specifications:

## Claude Opus 5.5

# bom-0-4 MW-class Cargo Tugs: Technical Proposal

**Phase 0B item, with Phase 0A design work**
**Proposed configuration baseline: TUG-BL-0. For review only; nothing here is approved.**

---

## 0. Executive summary

**What the tug does.** The tug is an uncrewed solar-electric vehicle. It shuttles pallets of reduced Fe-Ni product from the processing plant at the target NEA (bom-0-3) to the Phase 1 receiving node at SEL1 (bom-0-13). It then returns empty pallets and, optionally, small equipment.

**Recommended point design**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Array power | **1.5 MWe BOL at 1 AU**; ~1.1 MWe at 1 AU after 12 years |
| PPU input power | 1.2 MW nominal |
| Thrusters | 16 iodine Hall heads (15 active, 1 spare) in 4 pods |
| Specific impulse | 2,500 s nominal; throttleable 1,600–2,800 s |
| Thrust | ~57 N at 1.2 MW |
| Dry mass | 45 t (38–60 t) |
| Iodine capacity | 100 t, in swappable cassettes |
| Payload | 220 t nominal; 300 t rated at Δv ≤ 4.3 km/s per leg |
| Fleet | **12 tugs**, bought in two gated tranches (4 + 8) |
| Delivered product | **~0.95 kt/yr** (0.65–1.3 kt/yr) at a reference 2.5-year cycle |
| Fleet propellant demand | ~280 t/yr (200–450) |

**The opinion this design rests on.** At the reference target (3.5 km/s per leg), any vehicle above about 0.6 MW finishes its thrusting in under 1.3 years. The cycle is then set by trajectory windows, not by power. My own sizing supports Claude's round-2 critique on this point.

I still use MW-class power, which the binding range requires, for two things that do raise delivered tonnage per dollar:

1. **Window independence.** The tug carries the Δv capacity (≤ 5 km/s per leg) to depart off-optimum and still close a 2.5–3-year cycle. That widens the usable fraction of each synodic period and the set of eligible targets.
2. **Higher Isp.** Running at 2,500 s rather than ~2,000 s cuts propellant per cycle by about 15–20%. Propellant logistics, not vehicle capital, is the largest recurring cost of Phase 0 transport.

I therefore sit at the **low end of the 1.0–2.5 MWe range**, the knee of the curve (§4.3). The structure carries a growth scar to 2.0 MWe, to be activated only if the named-target trajectory study demands it.

**Cost of this item**

| Element | Point | Range |
|---|---|---|
| 0A design through PDR | $65M | $40–90M |
| 0B average unit recurring, arrays included | $280M | $175–450M |
| 0B item total (12 tugs, 28 pallets, GSE, sustaining) | $3.8B | $2.4–5.9B |

These figures exclude NRE (bom-0-11), launch (bom-0-8), propellant (bom-0-16), spares (bom-0-14) and operations (bom-0-10). §9 states the demand placed on each.

**Bottom line on economics.** Transport costs roughly **$0.6–1.2k per kg delivered** to SEL1. That is about parity with Starship-era Earth delivery, not a saving. This is consistent with D-01: Phase 0 transport is a **capability demonstration**.

---

## 1. Scope, boundaries and baseline control

### 1.1 In scope (bom-0-4)
- Tug vehicles (12 in the baseline), including their **own solar arrays**. Split accounting from bom-0-5 is agreed.
- **Product pallets** (reusable cargo frames) and the Pallet Standard Interface (PSI).
- The tug side of all interfaces: PSI latches, the propellant-cassette bay, the ORU (orbital replaceable unit) servicing interfaces and the docking target set.
- Tug-specific ground support equipment and the production line.
- Production-phase sustaining engineering.
- Phase 0A system design to PDR, with no flight hardware.

### 1.2 Out of scope (demand stated in §9, not costed here)

| Excluded scope | Owner |
|---|---|
| Thruster, array and feed qualification; the MW iodine test facility | bom-0-11 |
| Flight demonstration of a full wing and a thruster pod | bom-0-12 pathfinder |
| Launch and high-energy injection of tugs | bom-0-8 |
| Iodine supply, cassette filling and cassette ownership | bom-0-16 |
| Wear kits and spare heads | bom-0-14 |
| Servicing robotics, pallet storage and unloading at SEL1 | bom-0-13 |
| Product staging platform at the NEA | bom-0-3 |
| Ground segment and mission operations | bom-0-9, bom-0-10 |
| Contamination and disposal requirements (tug complies) | bom-0-15 |

### 1.3 Baseline control
- TUG-BL-0 supersedes the round-1 designs (800 kWe and 1.5 MW human-rated freighters) and the round-2 300 kWe / 15-vehicle concept.
- Those documents should be marked **SUPERSEDED**. They describe a different architecture: a cislunar station fed with ore.
- No crew provisions are carried. I keep only generic docking, power and data interfaces and structural reserve, not a "human-rating" label (§5.8).

---

## 2. Design philosophy

1. **Size power to the Δv envelope and the cycle, not to the reference target.** Throughput is window-limited. Surplus power is spent on Isp and window flexibility, not on speed.
2. **No fluid or solid propellant transfer in Phase 0.** Iodine travels in sealed, swappable 10 t cassettes. This turns the T14 transfer problem into a mechanism problem, which is easier to qualify.
3. **Wear parts are consumables.** Hall-thruster wear kits (pole covers, cathode, gas distributor, channel inserts) are swapped robotically at SEL1 every cycle. No head is required to survive 15 years.
4. **The tug never touches the asteroid.** It captures a pallet from a staging platform at a standoff of 1 km or more. This keeps a 160 m, 4,600 m² vehicle out of dust, plume and regolith environments.
5. **Graceful degradation is free.** Because power is not the binding constraint, losing a head, a pod or even a wing costs schedule margin, not deliveries.
6. **Node-agnostic.** Swapping SEL1 for SEL2, EML1 or a high Earth orbit changes low-thrust Δv by about 0.1–0.5 km/s, which is inside the envelope. D-04 can be re-decided at the 0B gate without redesign.
7. **Propellant-agnostic until PDR.** There is a common spine and power/propulsion architecture, with two feed-module variants: Iodine Feed Module (IFM, the reference) and Argon Feed Module (AFM, the alternate), per D-05.

---

## 3. Mission concept

### 3.1 Reference cycle (2.5 years)

```
 SEL1 node                                          Target NEA (co-located plant)
 ─────────                                          ─────────────────────────────
 [Service 30–45 d]                                  
   • drop loaded pallet                             
   • take empty pallet                              
   • swap 6–10 iodine cassettes                     
   • swap 15 wear kits (robotic, bom-0-13)          
        │                                           
        │  OUTBOUND  ~0.7–0.9 yr  (thrust ~0.25 yr, coast/phase rest)
        │  m0 ≈ 115 t (45 dry + 6 pallet + ~60 I2 + ≤20 t optional equipment)
        └──────────────────────────────────────────►  [Prox ops 30–90 d]
                                                       • holds 10 km/1 km/100 m/20 m
                                                       • drop empty pallet, capture loaded
                                                         pallet at staging platform ≥1 km
                                                       • (optional) deliver site equipment
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────◄
        │  RETURN  ~0.9–1.1 yr  (thrust ~0.65 yr)
        │  m0 ≈ 315 t (45 dry + 220 t product + 6 t pallet + ~45 t I2)
        ▼
 [Window margin / phasing ~0.3–0.5 yr]
```

### 3.2 Design-reference Δv
- **Reference:** 3.5 km/s per leg (low-thrust, node ↔ NEA), 7 km/s round trip.
- **Envelope:** 5 km/s per leg (10 km/s round trip). This covers off-optimal departures, a poorer target, or GPT's 8 km/s reference with margin.
- **Assumption A-01:** the target-gate trajectory study (Copernicus or EMTG on the named target) confirms a cycle of 3.0 years or less at 5 km/s per leg or less. This is the single most important unverified assumption (§12, OQ-1).

---

## 4. Technical specification

### 4.1 Top-level specification (TUG-BL-0)

| Array power, BOL at 1 AU | 1.50 MWe | 4 wings × 1,152 m² at ~330 W/m² BOL at operating temperature |

| Power at 1.2 AU | ~0.72 × the 1 AU value | 1/r², partly offset by cooler cells |
| PPU input, nominal | 1.2 MW; 1.0 MW from year ~8 | ~100 kW reserved for housekeeping, feed heaters, thermal, margin |
| Bus | 300 V-class array bus; SiC discharge converters ≥ 97% | Direct-drive at ~600 V is an option after plasma-arcing tests |
| Thrusters | 16 nested-channel Hall heads, 100 kW rated, 80 kW nominal at 600 V | 15 active, 1 hot spare; magnetically shielded |

| Thrust | 57 N at 1.2 MW and 2,500 s; ~95 N in high-thrust mode at 1,600 s | F = 2ηP/vₑ |
| Mass flow | 2.32 g/s (73 t/yr continuous) | |
| Dry mass | 45 t (38–60) | §4.4, including 20% margin |
| Iodine capacity | 100 t (10 cassettes × 10 t; 20.3 m³) | Envelope case 85 t + 5 t reserve |
| Payload | 220 t nominal; 300 t at ≤ 4.3 km/s per leg | §4.2 |

| Max acceleration (empty) | ~5×10⁻⁴ m/s² | Loads are trivial; launch loads govern structure |
| Design life | 15 yr / 6 cycles; ORU-serviceable | |
| Wing span | ~160 m tip-to-tip; spine ~40 m | |
| Stowed envelope | ≤ 8 m diameter × ≤ 18 m | Super-heavy fairing class |
| Battery | 50 kWh Li-ion | Safe mode and shadow excursions only |
| Waste heat to radiators | ~60 kWt (100 kWt design) | Pumped single-phase loop, ~160 m² |

### 4.2 Propellant and Δv budget (Isp 2,500 s, vₑ = 24.5 km/s, dry 45 t, pallet 6 t)

| Case | Return final mass | Return I₂ | Outbound final mass | Outbound I₂ | Burned | Loaded (incl. reserve) | Thrust time* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Reference: 220 t, 3.5 km/s per leg | 271 t | 41.6 t | 96 t | 14.7 t | 56 t | **~60 t** | 0.93 yr |
| 300 t, 3.5 km/s per leg | 351 t | 53.9 t | 109 t | 16.7 t | 71 t | 75 t | 1.17 yr |
| Envelope: 220 t, 5 km/s per leg | 271 t | 61.3 t | 117 t | 26.5 t | 88 t | 93 t | 1.45 yr |
| 300 t, 4.3 km/s per leg (rated limit) | 351 t | 66.3 t | 121 t | 23.0 t | 89 t | 94 t | 1.47 yr |

\*Thrust time divides burned propellant by 73 t/yr and by an average power factor of 0.83 (heliocentric distance plus duty).

**Argon alternate (AFM).** Assumptions: Isp ~2,900 s, η ~0.45, thrust ~37 N at 1.2 MW, dry mass +7 t for supercritical COPVs (~125 m³ at 300 bar) or +5 t for a cryogenic tank with a 1–2 kW cryocooler. At the reference Δv the AFM burns ~50 t/cycle with ~1.6 years of thrusting, which closes. At the 5 km/s envelope it needs ~2.4 years of thrusting, which does **not** close a 2.5–3-year cycle. Argon therefore shrinks the target envelope; it does not end the programme.

### 4.3 Why 1.5 MWe? (power trade, reference payload 220 t)

| Array BOL | Ops power | Dry | Ref thrust time | Envelope thrust time | Envelope fits 2.5–3 yr cycle? | Unit cost Δ vs 1.5 MWe |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.0 MWe | 0.8 MW | 39 t | 1.3 yr | 2.0 yr | No | −$45M |
| **1.5 MWe** | **1.2 MW** | **45 t** | **0.9 yr** | **1.4 yr** | **Yes, ~1 yr margin** | 0 |
| 2.0 MWe | 1.6 MW | 51 t | 0.7 yr | 1.1 yr | Yes | +$50M |
| 2.5 MWe | 2.0 MW | 57 t | 0.6 yr | 0.9 yr | Yes | +$100M |

- Going from 1.5 to 2.5 MWe saves about 0.3–0.5 years of thrusting inside a cycle that is window-limited anyway.
- That costs about $1.2B across 12 tugs (+$100M each), and buys throughput only if the window study shows windows narrower than ~1.5 years.
- 1.5 MWe is therefore the knee. The 2.0 MWe growth scar (a fifth and sixth wing, PPU slots, radiator area reserve) costs about 1.5 t and $5M per tug, and preserves the option.

**Mass properties**
- Loaded CG sits about 20 m forward of the pods.
- A 0.3 m lateral CG error in the pallet needs about 0.9° of gimbal, well inside ±10°.
- The first array mode is expected at ~0.03–0.08 Hz. Attitude control uses notch filters and slow thrust vectoring, plus two double-gimbal CMGs for the roll axis.

---

## 5. Subsystem breakdown

### 5.1 Electric propulsion (T01)

**Head**
- Nested two-channel, magnetically shielded Hall thruster, 100 kW rated, run at 80 kW and 600 V (~133 A).
- Derating trades thrust density for life, which is acceptable because the system is power-rich.

**Cluster**
- 4 pods × 4 heads. Each pod has its own PPU string.
- One head failing costs 1/15 of thrust. Losing one pod still leaves 0.9 MW of usable power.

**Life**
- Reference cycle: ~3.7 t per head. Envelope cycle: ~5.9 t per head.
- **Requirement:** qualified throughput of **≥ 6 t I₂ per wear-kit interval**. With a 1.5× life factor, that means ≥ 9 t demonstrated by test plus erosion modelling.
- Context: NEXT demonstrated 918 kg; HERMeS projects more than 1.7 t on xenon. 9 t is therefore a step change. It depends on magnetic shielding moving the life limit from the channel to replaceable pole covers and the cathode.
- Wear kits are swapped every cycle, so fleet demand is **~72 kits/yr plus ~5 replacement heads/yr**.

**Cathode**
- Iodine poisons BaO dispensers. The baseline is LaB₆ or C12A7-electride cathodes on iodine.
- **Fallback:** a 3 t noble-gas cathode-feed tank (Kr or Ar, ~5% of flow, ~15 t/yr fleet-wide).
- This must be decided by the T01 TRL-5 milestone.

**Throttle modes**
- High-Isp (2,800 s) for cruise when windows allow.
- High-thrust (1,600 s, ~95 N) for window catch-up and prox-ops collision avoidance. At 315 t this gives 0.1 m/s in about 5 minutes.

### 5.2 Power (T02)

**Arrays**
- Four flexible blanket wings, each 16 m × 72 m (rolled or Z-folded).
- Cells: IMM or multijunction at ≥ 30%. Packing factor 0.9.
- Wings are ORU-replaceable at the node, as a contingency and not a planned swap.

**Electrical**
- 300 V-class strings, plasma-hardened against arcing: grouted interconnects, no exposed conductor above ~100 V differential.
- Discharge converters are SiC at ≥ 97%. Magnet, keeper and heater supplies are conventional.

**Environment**
- Specific risk: iodine back-flow deposition on cover glass (contamination allowance 5%).
- Plume geometry and the "edge-on" pod cant are design drivers.

**Other power functions**
- **No dockside power** is required at the node or the NEA; the tug is always self-powered.
- **Option (not baselined):** a 200 kW power-export port through the PSI, for contingency support of the node or the plant. It is flagged OQ-9.

### 5.3 Thermal (T03 at tug level)
- Heat load: PPU losses ~36 kW, avionics and battery ~5 kW, back-conduction from thruster mounts ~15 kW, feed-heater loss ~4 kW, giving ~60 kWt. The design point is 100 kWt.
- Rejection: a single-phase pumped loop at 40–60 °C feeding ~160 m² of two-sided radiators, edge-on to the sun. ISS-ETCS-class heritage puts this at TRL 5–6 today.
- About 480 kW of thruster loss leaves through the plume and by direct radiation from the heads. It is a **geometry** problem (view factors to arrays and radiators), not a radiator-sizing problem.
- **Position:** T03 is project-ending for the plant (bom-0-3, bom-0-5) but **not for the tug**. I propose reclassifying the tug instance of T03 to "architecture-change, AD² 4". The plant's T03 retires the shared risk.

### 5.4 Propellant storage and feed (T14)

**Iodine Cassette Module (ICM)**
- 10 t solid I₂ (2.03 m³) in a Hastelloy- or Ti-lined shell with integral heaters, ~0.25 t empty.
- Fluid connections: one sublimation outlet with dual valves. Mechanical: a 4-point berthing latch with a power/data connector.

**Feed**
- Iodine is heated in the cassette to give ~2.3 g/s of vapour through heated lines (150–180 °C) to the pod flow controllers.
- Sublimation power is 0.57 kW (246 kJ/kg × 2.32 g/s). Including line and valve heaters the total is ~3 kW.

**Bay and swap**
- The tug has 10 slots. A typical cycle swaps 6–10 cassettes at SEL1 using the node manipulator (bom-0-13).
- Empty cassettes are left at the node for refill (vapour transfer) or retirement under bom-0-16 and bom-0-15. They are **never released**.

**Material compatibility**
- No aluminium in wetted paths. Seals are PTFE/FFKM qualified for multi-year iodine exposure.

### 5.5 Payload handling (T12)

**Product pallet**
- Reusable Ti-Al truss frame, ~6 t. Envelope ≤ 6 m diameter × 4 m.
- Holds up to 300 t of Fe-Ni billets, e.g. ~440 billets of 500 kg (220 t ≈ 28 m³ at 7.9 g/cm³), each with dual restraint.
- Pallet pool: 2 × fleet + 4 = **28 pallets**.

**Pallet Standard Interface (PSI)**
- 4 m androgynous ring with 4 structural latches and a compliant soft-capture stage.
- Capture rated for ≤ 2 cm/s closing speed: 20 J at 100 t.
- Two-fault-tolerant against inadvertent release: three independent inhibits, consistent with D-03 ALARP.

**Product acceptance specification (tug requirement on bom-0-3)**

| Item | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Mass | ≤ 300 t, certified to ±1% |
| CG | Within 0.25 m of the PSI axis |
| Loose particulates | None > 1 mm |
| Outgassing | Below the bom-0-15 limit |
| Fiducials | Passive retroreflectors and AprilTag-class targets on every pallet |

**At the NEA**
- The tug docks to the pallet held on the plant's staging platform, which stays ≥ 1 km from the surface in a terminator or hover station.
- The tug does **not** carry a manipulator for this.
- If bom-0-3 cannot provide a staging platform, the fallback is a 1.5 t tug-mounted capture arm pair. That is an architecture change; see OQ-3.

### 5.6 GNC and navigation (T25)

**Cruise**
- Onboard low-thrust guidance (Dawn-heritage approach) with weekly ground ephemeris and trajectory updates.
- Radiometric navigation (X-band, ΔDOR as needed) plus optical navigation against stars and the target.

**NEA approach**
- Optical navigation, then shape-model-relative navigation.
- Flash lidar (≤ 5 km) and fiducial tracking of the staging platform and pallet.
- Holds at 10 km, 1 km, 100 m and 20 m.
- Autonomous abort to a passively safe trajectory: high-thrust EP mode plus RCS.

**SEL1**
- Halo station-keeping (~2–10 m/s/yr) and node-relative navigation using cooperative targets.
- Plume keep-out: no firing above 10 kW within a 30° cone of the node inside 5 km. This is a bom-0-15 interface value.

**Attitude**
- Gimbal thrust-vector control in cruise. CMGs for roll. RCS for prox ops when EP is off.
- Sun-safe mode needs < 5 kW, met from arrays or the battery.

### 5.7 Avionics, autonomy and FDIR
- Radiation-tolerant dual-string computers with cross-strapping. A separate prox-ops computer handles lidar and vision.
- **Autonomous FDIR:**
  - head drop-out and cluster rebalance within 60 s;
  - PPU string isolation;
  - wing fault isolation;
  - cassette heater fault and changeover;
  - autonomous retreat to safe trajectories during prox ops.
- **Ground role:** go/no-go at each prox-ops hold, plus weekly cruise updates. Light-time to the NEA is 8–17 minutes one way at 1–2 AU, so everything below the 100 m hold is onboard-closed-loop.

### 5.8 Interfaces kept in place of "human-rating"
- One generic standard docking interface (IDSS-compatible geometry, ~0.4 t), used for node berthing. It is not crew-rated.
- Standard power and data connectors on the PSI and the ORUs.
- No 3 g load case, no crew kits, no shelter.
- I side with Claude and GPT. The extra mass is ~0.4 t (1% of dry mass) and buys servicing access now. It does not imply any crew capability.

### 5.9 Communications (bom-0-9 interface)

**Hardware:** X-band TT&C on LGAs and the HGA; Ka-band data on a 2.0 m HGA with a 50 W TWTA.

**Link estimate (Ka, 32 GHz, 2.0 m HGA ≈ 54 dBi)**

| 2 AU | 34 m (~79 dBi), C/N₀ ≈ 66 dB-Hz | ~1.4 Mbps |
| 2 AU | 18 m commercial | ~350 kbps |
| 1 AU | 18 m commercial | ~1.4 Mbps |

**Demand**

## 12. Open engineering questions

1. **OQ-1, cadence.** For the named target, what is the minimum cycle at ≤ 5 km/s per leg, and how much of each synodic period is usable? This decides fleet size and whether the 2.0 MWe scar is used.
2. **OQ-2, life.** What throughput per wear kit can a magnetically shielded iodine Hall head reach at 600 V? Is the life limiter the pole cover, the cathode or the channel?
3. **OQ-3, staging.** Will bom-0-3 provide a pallet staging platform at ≥ 1 km? If not, does the tug carry capture arms (+1.5 t, architecture change)?
4. **OQ-4, cathode gas.** Pure iodine, or a noble-gas cathode feed? This affects bom-0-16 and D-05.
5. **OQ-5, Isp optimum.** Including delivered propellant price, is 2,500 s right, or does 2,800 s at higher voltage pay off despite life risk?
6. **OQ-6, ICM refill.** Can empty cassettes be refilled at SEL1 by vapour transfer, or are they single-trip? This affects debris, mass delivered and bom-0-16 cost.
7. **OQ-7, contamination.** What iodine deposition rate on cover glass and node surfaces is acceptable, and does it rise with fleet traffic at the node?

## Gemini 3.1 Pro

# Technical Proposal: MW-class Cargo Tugs (bom-0-4)
**Phase 0B - Space Resource Processing**

## 1. Recommended Approach and Design Philosophy
The Phase 0B cargo transport architecture relies on a fleet of uncrewed, high-power Solar Electric Propulsion (SEP) tugs. Following the 2026 re-assessment, the design discards human-rating margins, crew habitats, and LOX/LH₂ propulsion. 

Our philosophy centers on **Modular Autonomy and High-Density Storage**. We baseline **Iodine (I₂)** as the propellant to bypass the cryogenic requirements of argon and the supply-chain impossibilities of xenon. To mitigate iodine's corrosive properties and lower TRL, the propulsion modules are designed as robotically replaceable Line Replaceable Units (LRUs). The tug operates as a continuous shuttle between the target NEA and the SEL1 delivery node, berthing with standardized 200-ton cargo containers via a despun interface.

## 2. Technical Specifications

*   **Fleet Size:** 15 operational vehicles
*   **Power Generation:** 1.5 MWe BOL (1 AU) via deployable flexible solar arrays
*   **Vehicle Dry Mass:** 38 t (excluding cargo)
*   **Propellant Capacity:** 75 t (Iodine, stored as solid, sublimated via waste heat)
*   **Payload Capacity:** 200 t (Fe-Ni product in standardized containers)
*   **Propulsion:** 10x 150 kW Magnetically Shielded Hall Effect Thrusters (8 active, 2 spare)
*   **Thrust & Isp:** ~28 N total thrust at 2,100 s Isp
*   **Round-trip Δv:** ~6.5 km/s (Target dependent)
*   **Cycle Time:** ~2.5 - 3.0 years per round trip

## 3. System Architecture

The vehicle is built around a central titanium/composite truss. The forward section houses the despun docking interface and avionics. The mid-section holds the solid iodine tanks and deployable solar arrays. The aft section houses the Power Processing Units (PPUs), deployable radiators, and the thruster LRUs.

### 3.1 Propulsion physics

For electrical input \(P\), bus-to-directed-jet efficiency \(\eta\), and exhaust velocity \(v_e\):

\[
v_e=g_0I_{sp}
\]

\[
T=\frac{2\eta P}{v_e}
\]

At:

- \(P=2.0\) MW,
- \(\eta=0.60\),
- \(I_{sp}=2,500\) s,

the effective exhaust velocity is approximately 24.5 km/s, giving:

\[
T\approx98\ \mathrm{N}
\]

and:

\[
\dot m=\frac{T}{v_e}\approx0.0040\ \mathrm{kg/s}
\]

That is approximately **345 kg/day during powered operation**.

These are first-order propulsion values. They do not establish transfer duration or accessibility.

### 3.2 Correct accounting of outbound and return propellant

The outbound leg carries the propellant needed for the loaded return. Ignoring this materially understates departure mass.

For a 70 t dry tug, 250 t product load, 6 t retained reserve, and a 4 km/s loaded return:

\[

=(70+250+6)
\left[\exp\left(\frac{4}{24.5}\right)-1\right]
\approx58\ \mathrm{t}
\]

The outbound leg must accelerate the dry tug, retained reserve, and return propellant:

\[
m_{p,\mathrm{out}}
=(70+6+58)
\left[\exp\left(\frac{3}{24.5}\right)-1\right]
\approx17\ \mathrm{t}
\]

Thus the reference cycle requires approximately:

- **75 t burned**.
- **81 t initially loaded**, including retained reserve.
- **151 t departure mass** from the delivery node.
- **384 t mass after product pickup at the NEA**.
- **326 t arrival mass**, including product and retained reserve.

This calculation assumes no major equipment cargo outbound. Such cargo must be manifested and recomputed explicitly.

- Normal loading around 81 t.
- Approximately ten 20 t-class storage modules, or an equivalent subdivided arrangement.
- Multiple feed paths with isolation.
- Controlled thermal gradients to prevent unwanted deposition.

- Passive isolation after a feed-system failure.

1. Establish an approved relative trajectory outside the node keep-out region.
2. Terminate EP and verify isolation.
3. Acquire independent relative-navigation solutions.
4. Enter a hold point.
5. Receive node authorization to continue.
6. Approach at low relative speed.
7. Capture, structurally secure, and unload propulsion control.
8. Verify power, data, and cargo-transfer state.

**Indicative duration: 2–4 years, partly parallel.**

Demonstrate:

- Representative high-power thruster/PPU strings.
- Representative propellant feed and storage behavior.
- High-voltage array sectors and deployment hardware.
- Full-scale radiator-loop elements.
- Cargo capture and restraint mechanisms.
- Hardware-in-the-loop autonomous navigation.

#### Stage C — Relevant-environment qualification

Required evidence includes:

| Technology | Required 0A evidence before 0B commitment |
|---|---|
| T01 MW EP cluster | Representative strings plus MW-level integration, interactions, faults, throughput/life evidence |
| T02 MW deployable arrays | Deployment, HV operation, structural dynamics and environment evidence representative of the flight design |
| T03 Heat rejection | Flight-relevant thermal rejection, loop operation, freeze/restart and fault isolation |
| T12 Heavy cargo handling | Validated full-mass dynamics plus relevant-environment capture/transfer evidence |
| T14 Large propellant system | Full-scale storage/feed architecture evidence, validated scaling and relevant-environment fluid/solid behavior |
| T25 Navigation/control | End-to-end autonomous navigation and proximity operations in representative flight conditions |

A ground crane moving a 250 t test mass is not equivalent to microgravity handling. Conversely, a small orbital demonstration cannot by itself validate full-mass flexible-body dynamics. Both evidence types are required.

For T14, ground proof of 200 t structural capacity must be combined with representative low-gravity feed and thermal demonstrations. If the assessment authority concludes that the chosen flight demonstration is not representative, **KDP-0B waits**.

#### Stage D — Flight demonstrator

The demonstrator should test:

- Flight-representative array deployment and high-voltage behavior.
- Integrated power/propulsion/thermal operation.
- Autonomous navigation and safe approach/retreat.
- Propellant feed behavior.
- Robotic replacement interfaces.
- Cargo capture using an appropriately scaled inertial article.

The flight programme must be capable of establishing the required TRL, not merely generating attractive imagery.

### 10.3 KDP-0B discriminating gates

Production commitment requires all four:

1. **Target gate:** accessible resource, verified product potential, and optimized transport schedule.
2. **Demand gate:** signed Phase 1 material, purity, mass, and date commitments.
3. **Economics gate:** explicit comparison against Earth supply, including the value of capability development.
4. **Licence gate:** acceptable collision, debris, contamination, disposal, and jurisdictional arrangements.

If a project-ending technology fails, use the agreed Earth-supplied-material fallback or reconsider the transport architecture. Do not convert a failed demonstration into a readiness waiver.

---

## 11. Cost estimate and accounting

### 11.1 Estimate basis

All figures are **rough-order-of-magnitude, constant 2026 USD**.

They are not supplier quotations.

Array hardware uses the binding reassessment allowance of **$30–150/W**, with launch separately accounted. The reference array has approximately **4.8 MW BOL output at 1 AU**.

This rating basis matters: pricing only “2 MW” would undercount the hardware needed to provide 2 MW propulsion power at 1.3 AU EOL.

### 11.2 Recurring vehicle hardware

| Element | Unit range |
|---|---:|
| Solar-array hardware | $144–720M |
| Structure, docking and cargo load path | $35–60M |
| Thrusters, PPUs and gimbals | $100–170M |
| Propellant storage and feed | $40–70M |
| Thermal system | $25–45M |
| Avionics, navigation and communications | $20–35M |
| Auxiliary systems and service interfaces | $20–35M |
| Assembly, integration and acceptance testing | $40–65M |
| **Total recurring vehicle** | **$424M–1.20B** |

Recommended budget shorthand: **$0.43–1.2B per vehicle**, with a **$0.65–0.85B working planning band** pending quotations.

The estimate includes the initial reusable carrier allocation. Spare carriers and replacement inventories require separate accounting.

### 11.3 Fleet procurement

| Fleet case | Recurring hardware envelope |
|---|---:|
| 12 vehicles | $5.2–14.4B |
| 14 vehicles | $6.0–16.8B |
| 16 vehicles | $6.9–19.2B |

At **14 vehicles × $0.75B**, the planning point is approximately **$10.5B**.

These totals exclude:

- Launch and delivery.
- Propellant procurement and delivery.
- Operations and ground infrastructure.
- Replacement inventory.
- NRE and pathfinder costs.
- Programme contingency and reserve.

### 11.4 Phase split and related allocations

| Phase/scope | Proposed range | Booked under |
|---|---:|---|
| 0A tug-related development and qualification | $1.2–3.0B | bom-0-11 |
| 0A tug-related flight demonstrator | $0.4–1.0B | bom-0-12 |
| 0A production fleet commitment | None | bom-0-4 |
| 0B recurring fleet, 12–16 vehicles | $5.2–19.2B | bom-0-4 |
| Launch/delivery, propellant, operations, spares | Separately estimated | Respective BOM items |

The **$1.6–4.0B tug-related 0A envelope** is an attribution to other programme lines, not an additional duplicate charge. Its split between development and flight hardware must be refined with the demonstrator design.

### 11.5 Disagreement with round-2 figures

I disagree with **$150–350M per MW-class tug including arrays** as a credible present planning allowance.

Reasons:

1. The specified service condition requires substantially more than 2 MW of 1 AU BOL array hardware.
2. At the agreed array pricing, the reference arrays alone cost **$144–720M**.
3. MW propulsion, large storage/feed systems, flexible spacecraft control, and robotic maintenance remain low-readiness developments.
4. Recurring hardware, NRE, launch, and replacement costs must be separated consistently.

I also reject high confidence in cycle time. The claimed power “knee” is unresolved until target-specific optimization exists. MW power substantially reduces thrust duration in this reference case; whether that reduction improves annual throughput remains a trajectory and scheduling question.

---

## 12. Reliability, maintenance, and spares

### 12.1 Maintenance concept

Service the tug at the receiving node where practical:

- Replace thruster/cathode assemblies.
- Exchange faulty PPUs.
- Inspect arrays and radiator loops.
- Exchange propellant modules.
- Check cargo fixtures.
- Update navigation and autonomy software.
- Recalibrate mass properties and thrust vectors.

The NEA site should support safing and essential diagnosis, but not be assumed to possess a complete tug overhaul facility.

### 12.2 Propulsion replacement demand

A reference tug completing approximately 6.5 cycles in 15 years would process about:

\[
6.5\times75\approx490\ \mathrm{t}
\]

Twenty-four installed strings sharing duty would average approximately **20 t per string** over that period.

A 10 t qualified throughput target therefore implies replacement during service life. At roughly 330 t/year fleet throughput:

\[
330/10\approx33
\]

The fleet consumes approximately **33 module-throughput equivalents per year**, before failures or uneven wear.

This is not necessarily 33 complete PPU replacements annually. The replaceable unit architecture must distinguish thruster head, cathode, gimbal, and electronics.

### 12.3 Fleet availability

The 85% reference availability is a requirement to be substantiated through:

- Reliability modelling.
- Maintenance-duration estimates.
- Spare inventory.
- Node servicing capacity.
- Fault-injection demonstrations.
- Actual early-flight performance.

Two reserve vehicles do not automatically guarantee 85% availability.

---

## 13. Safety, debris, and contamination

### 13.1 ALARP and interim limits

D-03 remains interim. Final limits require modelling, testing, and acceptance by the licensing state.

I recommend the following **proposed engineering allocation**, not a claim of approved regulation:

- No intentional release of product particles or hardware.
- Routine uncontained product loss below **\(10^{-6}\)** of handled product mass.
- Separate, more restrictive assessment of released objects or particles capable of hazardous impact.
- Two independent containment or restraint barriers where a single failure could release significant material.

For a 250 t shipment, the mass-fraction allocation is **0.25 kg**. That number alone is insufficient: particle size, velocity, persistence, and location also matter.

Compliance should use validated containment tests, particulate measurements, witness surfaces, and probabilistic models—not cargo weigh-in/weigh-out alone.

### 13.2 Additional controls

- EP prohibited within approved node and site plume-exclusion regions.
- Positive cargo-restraint verification before departure.
- Automatic retreat following inconsistent relative-navigation solutions.
- Propellant isolation following feed anomalies.
- Disposal planning that avoids persistent uncontrolled crossings of operational regions.
- Array and radiator impact-risk assessment.
- No routine venting of contaminated iodine-bearing material near operational infrastructure.

End-of-life disposal requires an approved trajectory and jurisdictional arrangement. “Leave it near L1” is not an acceptable disposal plan.

---

## 14. Principal risks

| Risk | Consequence | Mitigation and decision criterion |
|---|---|---|
| Target windows do not support required cadence | Fleet cannot meet delivery dates | Optimize named trajectories before production commitment |
| Iodine EP fails lifetime or contamination tests | Propellant/propulsion architecture change | Parallel argon assessment; no production down-select before evidence |
| Argon storage proves excessively heavy or costly | Alternate does not close | Price both storage approaches early |
| MW arrays fail deployment, HV, or dynamics requirements | Mission or programme loss | Sectorized deployment, representative flight evidence |
| Thermal losses exceed allocation | Propulsion derating | Integrated calorimetry and radiator testing |
| Large-scale propellant withdrawal is unstable | Loss of thrust capability | Full-scale feed hardware plus relevant microgravity tests |
| Cargo capture excites flexible modes | Contact damage or collision | Validated dynamics, low-speed capture, hold/abort logic |
| Dry-mass growth | More propellant, launch cost and cycle time | Protected mass allowance and recurrent mission reclosure |
| Servicing cannot be performed robotically | Availability collapse | End-to-end replacement demonstrations |
| Phase 1 demand is delayed or changes specification | Stranded fleet capacity | Demand gate and staged procurement |
| Programme cost exceeds capability value | Industrial option not exercised | Preserve 0B as a real option; retain Earth-supply fallback |

The largest near-term uncertainty is **not thrust calculation**. It is whether a particular target, delivery orbit, production schedule, and fleet can produce reliable dated deliveries.

---

## 15. Open engineering questions

Before preliminary design review, resolve:

1. **Which named NEA and SEL1 orbit define the actual mission?**
2. **How much does 2 MW improve delivery cadence relative to 1 MW and 2.5 MW?**
3. **What arrival schedule is achievable—not merely annualized throughput?**
4. **What product form and purity will Phase 1 sign for?**
5. **Can iodine meet representative throughput, restart, corrosion, and plume requirements?**
6. **What is the fully burdened argon alternate, including storage and refrigeration or pressure-vessel mass?**
7. **Can the 200 t-class storage architecture feed reliably at low acceleration and partial fill?**
8. **Which maintenance tasks must be demonstrated before deployment?**
9. **What packaged masses and injection orbits determine launch demand?**
10. **What evidence is sufficient for TRL 6 on full-scale heavy-cargo handling and large propellant systems?**
11. **What contamination and disposal limits will the licensing state accept?**
12. **What fleet capacity remains useful if production or demand ramps more slowly than planned?**

---

## Final recommendation

Adopt a **250 t payload, 2 MWe-at-1.3-AU-EOL tug** as the configuration-controlled engineering reference, with **14 vehicles as a provisional fleet planning point**.

Fund 0A to establish whether that reference is the right industrial solution. Do not authorize the fleet until target trajectories, representative technology demonstrations, signed demand, economics, and licensing all close.

For present budgeting, carry:

- **70 t reference dry mass**.
- **Approximately 75 t propellant burned per reference cycle**.
- **Approximately 1.1 kt/yr steady-state fleet delivery**, conditional on the assumed cycle.
- **$0.43–1.2B recurring hardware per tug**, including arrays.
- **$1.6–4.0B of tug-related 0A development and demonstrator activity**, booked in the appropriate shared BOM lines.

This is a challenging but technically structured transport programme. Its credibility depends on making power, propellant, heat, fleet scheduling, maintenance, and cost explicit—and allowing the 0B gate to say **no** if the evidence does not support industrial deployment.

## Key Specifications

- **Vehicle type and crewing:** All three models specify an uncrewed solar-electric cargo tug with no habitat, crew kits or life-support pass-throughs.
  - Claude and GPT explicitly reject the "human-rating" label and generic 3 g crew load cases.
  - Gemini also strips life-support from its docking port and keeps only structural, power and data linkages.
- **Reference propellant:** All three cost **solid iodine** as the reference case.
  - The iodine is sublimated and fed through heated lines with corrosion-resistant wetted materials: Hastelloy for Claude and Gemini (Claude also allows Ti), and compatibility-qualified materials for GPT.
  - Xenon is not baselined.
  - Claude and GPT carry argon as a costed alternate per D-05. Gemini does not develop an argon variant.
- **Propulsion architecture:** All three use a cluster of independently controlled **~100–150 kW thruster/PPU strings with installed spares**, not a single MW thruster. Wear-limited parts are robotically replaceable, mainly at the SEL1 node.
  - Claude: 16 × 100 kW Hall heads (15 active plus 1 spare), run at 80 kW.
  - Gemini: 10 × 150 kW Hall thrusters (8 active plus 2 spare).
  - GPT: 24 × 100 kW strings (20 active plus 4 spare); Hall versus gridded ion not yet selected.
- **Payload per loaded trip:** **200–250 t of reduced Fe-Ni product** (Claude 220 t, rated to 300 t; Gemini 200 t; GPT 250 t). It travels in a reusable carrier or pallet as billets or ingots, not loose powder.
- **Cycle time and delivered throughput:**
  - The reference round-trip cycle is **2.3–3.0 years** (Claude 2.5 yr; Gemini 2.5–3.0 yr; GPT 2.3 yr).
  - All models flag the cycle as unverified until a named-target trajectory study exists.
  - Fleet delivery converges on **~1 kt/yr**: Claude 0.95 (0.65–1.3); GPT 1.11 (0.80–1.35); Gemini's figures (15 × 200 t over 2.5–3.0 yr) imply roughly 1.0–1.2.
- **Propellant per cycle and design life:**
  - Reference propellant burned is **~55–80 t per cycle** (Claude ~56 t burned, 60 t loaded; GPT ~75 t burned, 81 t loaded; Gemini 75 t capacity).
  - Claude and GPT both carry a **15-year** service objective with consumable wear items. Gemini does not state a design life.
- **Safe-mode battery:** All three carry an onboard battery for safing and transients only, never for MW propulsion.
  - Claude and Gemini: 50 kWh.
  - GPT: 100–250 kWh.
- **Communications:** Cruise telemetry is in the tens to low hundreds of kbps, with proximity-operations bursts of **1–10 Mbps**.
  - Claude: 2–10 kbps averaged, with 50–200 kbps contacts and 1–5 Mbps in prox ops.
  - Gemini and GPT: 10–100 kbps in cruise and 1–10 Mbps in prox ops.
  - DSN is not assumed free. No continuous high-rate video is required.
- **Autonomy and proximity operations:** All three require onboard autonomous navigation and FDIR. This includes thruster drop-out and rebalance, and lidar plus optical relative navigation.
  - Claude and GPT add staged hold points, a ground go/no-go at each hold, EP shut-off or plume keep-out near the node, and autonomous passive-safe abort.
- **Top-ranked contamination risk:** All three rank iodine deposition and plume impingement on array cover glass and other surfaces as a top risk. Mitigation is through plume geometry and coupon testing.

## Divergent Views

- **Power rating basis and array size:** Claude recommends **1.5 MWe BOL at 1 AU** (~4,600 m², four wings). This gives ~1.1 MWe at end of life and ~0.72× that at 1.2 AU, with a 2.0 MWe growth scar. Gemini prefers **1.5 MWe BOL** from two 750 kWe roll-out wings of only ~3,500 m². GPT suggests specifying **2.0 MWe to propulsion at 1.3 AU, end of life**, which requires ~4.8 MW BOL at 1 AU and ~16,000 m² of array spanning 180–240 m.
  - Note: Gemini's stated 28 N at 2,100 s from ~1.2–1.5 MW implies only ~20% efficiency. The same power at the ~60% efficiency the other two assume would give ~85 N. Gemini's figure looks like an internal inconsistency.
- **Fleet size and procurement:** Claude recommends **12 tugs bought in gated tranches** of 4, then 8 (range 6–14), with Tranche 2 sized after the first full cycle. Gemini prefers **15 operational vehicles** in serial production from 2032. GPT suggests a **14-vehicle planning case** (12 in service plus 2 reserve, range 10–18), procured as 2 initial vehicles followed by lots of 3–4.
- **Dry mass and propellant storage:** Claude recommends **45 t dry (38–60)** with **100 t iodine** in ten swappable 10 t cassettes. Gemini prefers **38 t dry** with **75 t iodine** in fixed conformal tanks sublimated by PPU waste heat. GPT suggests **70 t dry (55–85)** with a deliberately oversized **200 t storage envelope** (60–70 m³), normally only partly filled.
- **Unit and fleet cost, including arrays:**
  - Claude recommends **$280M per unit ($175–450M)** and **$3.8B for the item ($2.4–5.9B)**, with $40–90M of 0A design to PDR. Arrays are priced at $40–100/W.
  - Gemini prefers **$220M per unit**, a **$3.3B fleet**, $1.2B NRE and ~$120M per vehicle for launch.
  - GPT suggests **$0.43–1.2B per unit** (working band $0.65–0.85B), a **~$10.5B fleet** at 14 × $0.75B, and $1.6–4.0B of tug-related 0A work booked in bom-0-11 and bom-0-12.
  - On the round-2 $150–350M per tug: Claude raises its top end to $450M; GPT rejects the range outright; Gemini's $220M sits within it.
- **Waste-heat rejection and T03 classification:** Claude recommends **~60 kWt (100 kWt design) on a ~160 m² single-phase pumped loop**. It argues most thruster loss leaves through the plume or by direct head radiation, so T03 for the tug should be reclassified to architecture-change, AD² 4. Gemini prefers rejecting **~400 kW through NaK-type liquid-metal loops**. GPT suggests a **0.45 MW-class active system with 600–1,000 m² of radiators** and insists every part of the ~0.8 MW of non-jet power be accounted for.
- **Bus voltage and dockside power:** Claude recommends a **300 V-class bus**, with direct drive at ~600 V only after arcing tests, **zero dockside power**, and an optional 200 kW export port. Gemini prefers **1–3 kV array output** fed directly to the PPUs, with **0.1 MW peak dockside power**. GPT suggests **1–3 kV as the starting trade** and a **100–250 kWe dockside service interface**.

## Open Questions

1. **Cycle time for a named target:**
   - What is the minimum round-trip cycle at ≤5 km/s per leg for a named NEA and a specified SEL1 halo orbit?
   - What fraction of each synodic period is usable?
   - Does any power above ~1 MWe raise delivered tonnage, given that thrusting takes only ~0.6–1.5 years inside a window-limited cycle?
   - All three models flag this question; it sets fleet size and the power point.
2. **Iodine thruster life:** Can a magnetically shielded thruster on iodine reach the required throughput?
   - Claude: ≥6 t per wear-kit interval, with ≥9 t demonstrated.
   - GPT: ~10 t per string, about 14,000 h.
   - Gemini: >10,000 h wear tests.
   - Sub-questions: is the life limiter the pole cover, the cathode or the channel, and does the BaO cathode need LaB₆/electride or a noble-gas cathode feed?
   - Context: present heritage is ~1–2 t on xenon. Gemini's "~70 t per vehicle" throughput is ambiguous against the ~490 t lifetime per vehicle implied by Claude and GPT.
3. **Large propellant storage and feed:**
   - Can tens to hundreds of tonnes of solid iodine be stored and sublimated reliably at 2–4 g/s in microgravity and at partial fill?
   - Can sealed cassettes be swapped robotically, or refilled at SEL1?
   - What is the fully burdened argon alternate? 200 t of liquid argon is ~143 m³ before tankage. Claude finds argon fails to close the 5 km/s-per-leg envelope.
4. **Contamination of arrays, radiators, optics and node surfaces:**
   - What iodine deposition rate is acceptable? Claude sets a <5% end-of-life power-loss criterion.
   - Does deposition scale with fleet traffic at the node?
   - What plume keep-out geometry is required?
5. **Heavy-cargo capture and flexible-body control:**
   - How should a 300–400 t vehicle with 160–240 m flexible wings (first modes ~0.03–0.08 Hz) capture a pallet?
   - What evidence counts as TRL 6 when ground tests cannot reproduce full-mass microgravity dynamics?
   - Who provides the NEA staging platform? Claude's design assumes a ≥1 km standoff platform from bom-0-3. Gemini contemplates docking and LRU swaps at the NEA.
6. **Launch packaging and injection:** How are stowed vehicles of 38–70 t dry, plus initial propellant, packaged for launch?
   - Claude: ≤8 m × 18 m stowed, ~65 t per launch, injected at C3 ≥ −2 km²/s² with no MW deployment in LEO.
   - GPT: multi-launch assembly may be needed.
   - Who supplies high-energy injection, at what price?

## Recommended Approach

1. **Freeze one baseline, TUG-BL-0, with power specified at a stated distance and age.** Adopt GPT's rule: propulsion input is specified at a stated heliocentric distance (e.g., 1.3 AU) and at end of life.
   - Carry a provisional point of **~1.2–2.0 MWe to the PPUs at that condition**.
   - Size the array from that point. This implies roughly 2.5–4.8 MW BOL at 1 AU, which is larger than Claude's and Gemini's 1.5 MWe BOL.
   - Keep Claude's growth scar so the point can move within 1.0–2.5 MWe once the named-target trajectory study (OQ-1) reports.
   - Mark the round-1 800 kWe and 1.5 MW human-rated freighters, and the 300 kWe concept, as superseded.
2. **Use a modular, power-rich propulsion cluster.**
   - Use 15–24 strings of ~100 kW with N+1 to N+4 spares, independent PPU and feed isolation, and robotically swappable wear kits treated as consumables.
   - Run at **~2,500 s Isp** to cut propellant, the dominant recurring cost.
   - Throttle down to ~1,600 s for window catch-up and collision avoidance.
   - Set a qualification target of **≥9–10 t of iodine throughput per wear-kit or string interval**, with the wear test started by 2030.
3. **Adopt sealed, swappable iodine cassettes and size storage to the Δv envelope.**
   - Use sealed swappable cassettes (Claude and GPT), not open bulk-solid transfer.
   - Carry **~100–150 t installed capacity**. This covers a 5 km/s-per-leg envelope without GPT's full 200 t penalty and can be revisited after T14 tests.
   - Keep an Argon Feed Module variant to PDR per D-05, and use the iodine variant for facility planning. Claude notes iodine's condensability makes MW-class ground testing feasible.
4. **Carry a realistic cost and procure in gated tranches.**
   - Budget **~$0.3–0.8B per unit including arrays**. Treat Gemini's $220M and the low end of round-2 ($150M) as not closing at the agreed $30–150/W once arrays are rated at the operating condition.
   - Carry a **0B item total of ~$3–10B**, with 0A tug design to PDR at **$40–90M** in bom-0-4. Book qualification and the pathfinder in bom-0-11 and bom-0-12.
   - Procure **2–4 vehicles at KDP-0B**. Size the remaining tranche (to a total of 10–18) only after the first full cycle has shown real cycle time, wear-kit life and signed Phase 1 demand.
5. **Close the full thermal ledger before PDR.**
   - Account for all non-jet power (~0.5–0.8 MW per tug) across plume, direct head radiation and the active loop, verified by integrated calorimetry.
   - Size the active loop from that data, within a range of 100–450 kWt.
   - Reclassify tug T03 to architecture-change only if test data confirms Claude's low active-load estimate.
6. **Keep the tug off the asteroid surface and standardise interfaces.**
   - The tug captures pallets at a standoff staging point. This requires a new interface requirement on bom-0-3.
   - Use a heavy-cargo capture ring rated for ≤2 cm/s closing speed and two-fault-tolerant against inadvertent release (interim ≤10⁻⁴ per transfer).
   - Product acceptance specification: mass ±1%, CG within 0.25 m of the interface axis, no particulates larger than 1 mm, plus fiducials.
   - Carry a non-crew-rated generic service interface. Settle the dockside power question (0 to 250 kWe) jointly with bom-0-13.
7. **Pass demands to other lines and gate on evidence.**
   - **bom-0-16:** ~280–400 t/yr of iodine (envelope 150–600 t/yr) and a signed supply covering ≥5 years at a stated price.
   - **bom-0-14:** ~70 wear kits and ~5 heads per year.
   - **bom-0-15:** plume keep-out values and an end-of-life disposition, preferring retirement to the node as Phase 1 spares or feedstock.
   - **KDP-0B entry:** TRL 6 with no waivers on T01, T02, T14 and T25, which requires a pathfinder flying at least one full-scale wing and a multi-string pod. A named-target cycle of ≤3.0 years. Iodine contamination of arrays shown below 5% end-of-life power loss.
   - **Fallback:** Earth-supplied material if any of these fails.
   - **Framing:** transport at ~$0.6–1.2k/kg is a capability programme under D-01, not a cost saving.
